text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's Austrian newspapers:
DER STANDARD
- All civil servants are now threatening to strike in protest at government plans to change pension schemes in the public sector. The union will decide on measures against spending cuts on Monday.

- The government coalition of Social Democrats and People's Party passed a new foreigner law despite protests by opposition parties. Greens, Liberals and church organisations criticise the new law as too tough.
- Austria's postal service plans to cut 3,000 jobs by introducing more part-time work and offering redundancy. The scheme aims to prepare the company for going public.
- Austria's trade deficit jumped 14.3 percent to just over 100 billion schillings in 1996 due to higher imports from other EU members.
DIE PRESSE

- Westdeutsche Landesbank says it does not want to take control of Bank Austria. A planned share swap offer to Creditanstalt shareholders and Bank Austria's information policy were the main points raised at Bank Austria's shareholders' meeting.
- Plastics producer Semperit plans to raise its capital in order to pay for future acquisitions. The company expects record earnings this year.
- Industrialist Hannes Androsch plans to participate in Germany's salt producer Suedwestsalz with his own salt company Salinen AG.
- Insurer Interunfall expects premium earnings to be 17 percent lower this year than in 1996.
KURIER
- Government plans to reform state pensions will not bring any savings for the 1998 and 1999 budgets.
- The building industry fears the government will cut construction spending by one billion schillings in 1998.
- Post & Telekom Austria chief Josef Sindelka says a telecommunications law providing fair competition is necessary ahead of the company's going public.
SALZBURGER NACHRICHTEN

- Former Finance Minister Hannes Androsch says the government should create a foundation with central bank and Vienna holding company AVZ money. The foundation should finance a two billion schillings technology offensive.
WIRTSCHAFTSBLATT
- Upper Austria's energy provider OKA plans to build a power plant worth one billion schillings together with Salzburg energy provider SAFE.
- Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger's plans to raise state voucher fees would bring the government 1.5 billion schillings. Industry is protesting.
